Clarify the meaning of sentences with ambiguous pronouns.

Q: In the following sentences, explain the antecedent of the pronoun (which thing the pronoun refers to), or state that it is ambiguous.
Sentence: The chief told the counselor that they took the day off.
Options:
(A) The chief took the day off
(B) The counselor took the day off
(C) Ambiguous
A: (A)

Q: In the following sentences, explain the antecedent of the pronoun (which thing the pronoun refers to), or state that it is ambiguous.
Sentence: The manager sent a message to the secretary, but he didn't reply yet.
Options:
(A) The secretary didn't reply yet
(B) The manager didn't reply yet
(C) Ambiguous
A: (A)

Q: In the following sentences, explain the antecedent of the pronoun (which thing the pronoun refers to), or state that it is ambiguous.
Sentence: Bailey will plan to meet the director at his office
Options:
(A) It will be Bailey's office
(B) It will be the director's office
(C) Ambiguous
A: (C)

Q: In the following sentences, explain the antecedent of the pronoun (which thing the pronoun refers to), or state that it is ambiguous.
Sentence: Bailey planned to meet the director at his office
Options:
(A) The office was the director's office
(B) The office was Bailey's office
(C) Ambiguous
A:

action.content:
Based on the context of the previous examples and the specific linguistic nuances highlighted in your "Trial #2" reflection, here is the analysis:

In the sentence "Bailey planned to meet the director at his office," the verb **meet** implies a visit or an encounter where one party goes to the location of the other. Pragmatically, when someone plans to meet another person "at [someone's] office," the location almost invariably belongs to the person being met (the director), as that is the standard venue for such a meeting. While grammatically "his" could refer to Bailey, the semantic context of the action overrides the default grammatical proximity rule. Therefore, the most logical interpretation is that the office belongs to the director.

A: (A)
